title: The Invariant Interval
text:
Tuesday’s exit ticket


Why does the position \(x\) appear in an equation for time?


The answer: because simultaneity is frame-dependent. Two events at different \(x\) get different \(t'\) precisely because the frames disagree about which clocks are synchronised.

The loose version to watch for: “because space and time are the same thing.”
They are mixed by a boost, not identified. One sign in the matrix keeps them apart, and that sign is today.

title: The Invariant Interval
text:
Proper time is the interval









Go to the frame where both events happen at the same place — the one that rides along. There \(\Delta x' = 0\), so \(\Delta s^{2} = c^{2}\Delta\tau^{2}\).

The interval is the wristwatch time of whatever travels between the two events. \(\tau\) from L05 was today’s invariant all along — we just did not have its name.

The longest path is the straight one









The minus sign reverses the inequality: a detour through space costs proper time. Sitting still is the way to age the most.

title: The Invariant Interval
section: The scissors, and why nothing is at the crossing point
text:
The scissors, and why nothing is at the crossing point









Blades of length \(L\) meeting at angle \(\theta\) cross at \(x = L/\tan\theta\). As \(\theta \to 0\) the crossing point runs out without limit.

Standing at the crossing point — could you learn anything about the far ends of the blades faster than light?

title: The Invariant Interval
text:
The statement that actually holds


The slogan

“Nothing can travel faster than light.”

False as stated — the spot and the crossing point both do.

The theorem

No causal influence propagates outside the light cone.

True, and structural — it is what \(\Delta s^{2} \geq 0\) says.











The bound is on what can affect what — and \(\Delta s^{2}\) is how spacetime encodes it.

title: The Invariant Interval
text:
Minkowski, 1908



“Henceforth space by itself, and time by itself, are doomed to fade away into mere shadows, and only a kind of union of the two will preserve an independent reality.”

Einstein’s old mathematics teacher, three years after the 1905 paper, telling a room of natural scientists what the paper had actually been about.





He had called Einstein a “lazy dog” as a student. He also called this formulation “a revelation” — and Einstein initially dismissed the geometry as überflüssige Gelehrsamkeit, superfluous learnedness.

(b) No — so one frame must be wrong

“Fits” = “both ends inside at the same time” — a simultaneity claim, not an event. Frames may disagree about it, and no door ever touches the train.

title: Length Contraction
text:
Measured is not photographed











A photograph collects light that arrives together — emitted at different times from different depths. A fast sphere photographs as a rotated sphere, not a flattened one. Measuring and seeing are different verbs — L03’s oldest lesson.

title: Length Contraction
section: The man who almost had it
text:
The man who almost had it


1892: Lorentz and FitzGerald propose that motion through the ether physically squeezes matter by exactly \(1/\gamma\) — invented to rescue Michelson–Morley.
Right formula. Wrong story.





A physical squeeze would be one-sided — the “really moving” frame’s rods shrink. Einstein’s version is symmetric, needs no ether and no force, and follows from simultaneity alone.

section: Don’t take my word for it — Annalen der Physik 17, 891 (1905)
text:
Don’t take my word for it — Annalen der Physik 17, 891 (1905)


§1, p. 893 — the definition. There is our train:



§2, p. 897 — the punchline. And look what starts right below:




“We must bear in mind that all our judgments in which time plays a role are always judgments about simultaneous events. If, for instance, I say ‘that train arrives here at 7 o’clock,’ I mean something like this: ‘the pointing of the small hand of my watch to 7 and the arrival of the train are simultaneous events.’”

“So we see that we must not attach absolute meaning to the concept of simultaneity: two events which, viewed from one coordinate system, are simultaneous, can no longer be regarded as simultaneous when viewed from a system moving relative to it.” — and directly beneath it: §3, where the math starts.

Same apparatus. Same room. Different reports.



“The pattern did not change after moving 90°.”


“It appeared to change the first time but did not.”

“Changed during the rotation, different after.”




Nobody misreported. Every one of these is correct.

“What if there is ether — but it just never gets windy?”

title: The Relativity of Simultaneity

You synchronized two clocks with a flash at the midpoint.
Your friend, moving at \(0.6c\), said one was set too early.

Today: she is right. And so are you.

title: The Relativity of Simultaneity
text:
What Tuesday gave us


A frame is a lattice of rulers and synchronized clocks.
Each event is recorded by the local clock.
Synchronization is a definition: midpoint flash, equal paths.




Everything today is these three facts plus the second postulate. No new machinery.

The train









Lightning strikes both ends. Both of you are at the midpoint when it happens.







The strikes are events: one instant, one point at each end of the train.

title: The Relativity of Simultaneity
text:
Your account (platform)
Light from A and light from B each travel half the train’s length to reach you.
Equal distances. Equal speeds.

The two flashes reach you at the same instant.
You conclude: simultaneous.

title: The Relativity of Simultaneity
text:
Her account (train)
She is moving toward B and away from A.









The light from B has less ground to cover. It arrives first.

title: The Relativity of Simultaneity
text:
Both are right


Platform
Flashes arrive together Equal distances → simultaneous

Train
B arrives first Equal distances → B struck first


There is no fact of the matter about which came first.


“But what REALLY happened?” — the question has no answer, any more than “which end of this train is really the front?”

Stop drawing space. Start drawing space and time together.











Sitting still is a vertical line — you move through time, not space.

“The Experiments on the relative motion of the earth and ether have been completed and the result decidedly negative.”

title: The Null Result, and What It Cost
section: “The most famous failed experiment in history”
text:
“The most famous failed experiment in history”
It was not a failure.
Michelson himself was disappointed — he considered it a failure for years.
He was wrong about his own result.

A null result from an instrument sensitive enough to have seen the effect is a discovery.

title: The Null Result, and What It Cost
text:
What became of it






1907 — America’s first science Nobel: “for his optical precision instruments…” The ether experiment is not mentioned.
1902–04 — Morley and Miller do the seasonal repeats, bigger. Null.
1920s — Miller, alone on Mount Wilson, claims a positive signal.
1955 — traced to temperature gradients. Modern repeats: null, to parts in \(10^{18}\).



“Without your work, this theory would today be scarcely more than an interesting speculation.”
— Einstein, toasting Michelson, January 1931




Caltech, January 1931 — Michelson, Einstein, Millikan. Michelson died four months later.

title: The Null Result, and What It Cost
text:
What a null result destroys
No detectable ether wind — so something in the chain that predicted 0.4 fringes is false. There are only three ways out:

1. “Earth drags the ether along with it.” Then there is no wind at ground level, and the fringes rightly stay put. ✗ But dragged ether would also carry starlight along — and stellar aberration (Bradley’s tilted telescopes, from Tuesday) exists only if Earth moves through an undisturbed ether. One escape, two contradictory experiments.


2. “Motion through the ether squeezes the arms.” FitzGerald (1889) and Lorentz (1892): if the along-wind arm contracts by exactly \(\sqrt{1-v^2/c^2}\), the two delays cancel and the null is explained. ad hoc — a factor invented to erase this one experiment, with no mechanism and no independent prediction. But hold onto that factor: it is nearly right, for entirely different reasons — week 4.


3. “There is no ether.” Light needs no medium, and \(c\) is the same in every inertial frame. Einstein, 1905 — the only escape that predicts new physics instead of explaining away old data.

text:
Here is the story every documentary and most textbooks tell:
Michelson–Morley destroyed the ether — so Einstein invented relativity.

title: The Null Result, and What It Cost
text:
Einstein, 1905




Bern, Switzerland. Age 26.

Not a professor. A patent examiner, third class.
Reviews patent applications — many for electromagnetic devices and clock synchronization.
In one year, 1905, publishes four papers. Any one of them would have made a career.

title: The Null Result, and What It Cost
text:
What Einstein actually wrote





“It is known that Maxwell’s electrodynamics — as usually understood at the present time — when applied to moving bodies, leads to asymmetries which do not appear to be inherent in the phenomena.”
— Zur Elektrodynamik bewegter Körper, opening sentence, 1905




Not a word about Michelson–Morley. The paper mentions “unsuccessful attempts to discover any motion of the earth relative to the light medium” only in passing, a paragraph later.

Coil moves, magnet at rest
Charges move through \(\mathbf{B}\) → force \(q\mathbf{v}\times\mathbf{B}\) → current flows


Same current. Same experiment. Two completely different explanations.

text:
Two postulates

1. The laws of physics are the same in every inertial frame.
2. The speed of light in vacuum is the same in every inertial frame, regardless of the motion of the source or the observer.


The first is old — Galileo would have signed it.
The second is the radical one.

Hendrik Lorentz




Wrote down the transformation equations (1892–1904) — before Einstein.
Believed length contraction was a real physical compression of matter moving through the ether.


“The chief cause of my failure was my clinging to the idea that the variable \(t\) only can be considered as the true time, and that my local time \(t'\) must be regarded as no more than an auxiliary mathematical quantity.”
— Lorentz, The Theory of Electrons, 1915 edition

title: The Null Result, and What It Cost
text:
Henri Poincaré




Argued simultaneity is a convention. Saw the group structure. And in September 1904 — a year early — said this:


“… the principle of relativity, according to which the laws of physical phenomena should be the same, whether for an observer fixed, or for an observer carried along in a uniform movement of translation.”
— Poincaré, address at St. Louis, September 1904

So why Einstein?
Lorentz had the mathematics. Poincaré had the principle, and the name.

They had the mathematics. Einstein supplied the meaning: no ether, no mechanism — just two postulates and the courage to follow them.

The equations


Differential
\(\nabla\cdot\mathbf{E}=\rho/\varepsilon_0\)
\(\nabla\cdot\mathbf{B}=0\)
\(\nabla\times\mathbf{E}=-\partial\mathbf{B}/\partial t\)
\(\nabla\times\mathbf{B}=\mu_0\mathbf{J}+\mu_0\varepsilon_0\,\partial\mathbf{E}/\partial t\)

The ether wind


If the ether is at rest and Earth orbits through it at 30 km/s, then from Earth’s frame there is a wind of ether streaming past.
Light should travel at \(c+v\) downwind, \(c-v\) upwind — like sound in moving air.






Earth's orbital speed:      v = 29,800 m/s
Ratio:                    v/c = 9.94e-05
Effect on travel time:  (v/c)² = 9.88e-09

A one-part-in-a-hundred-million effect.
No clock in 1887 could do that. No ruler could do that.



Aberration — the same effect that later ruled out ether drag.

title: How This Course Works — and the Ether Problem
text:
A swimmer moves at speed \(c\) relative to the water. A river flows at speed \(v\).

Swimmer A swims 100 m downstream, then back.
Swimmer B swims 100 m across, then back.

Who returns first?
(a) A    (b) B    (c) They tie    (d) Depends on \(v\)

title: How This Course Works — and the Ether Problem
section: Why the river matters going across
text:
Why the river matters going across
She cannot aim straight across — the current would carry her downstream.
She must aim upstream and let the current push her back onto the line.












Only \(\sqrt{c^2-v^2}\) is left for actually crossing.

The river costs her both ways — just less than it costs the downstream swimmer.

title: How This Course Works — and the Ether Problem
text:
Downstream and back — the derivation
Each leg is just distance over speed. Only the speed relative to the bank changes.
\[t_\parallel=\underbrace{\frac{L}{c+v}}_{\text{with the current}}
            +\underbrace{\frac{L}{c-v}}_{\text{against it}}\]

Common denominator \((c+v)(c-v)=c^2-v^2\):
\[t_\parallel=\frac{L(c-v)+L(c+v)}{c^2-v^2}=\frac{2Lc}{c^2-v^2}\]


Divide top and bottom by \(c^2\):
\[t_\parallel=\frac{2L}{c}\cdot\frac{1}{1-v^2/c^2}\]

title: How This Course Works — and the Ether Problem
text:
Across and back — the derivation
Effective crossing speed is \(\sqrt{c^2-v^2}\) — from the triangle.
Both legs are the same, so:
\[t_\perp=\frac{2L}{\sqrt{c^2-v^2}}\]

Factor \(c^2\) out of the square root:
\[\sqrt{c^2-v^2}=c\sqrt{1-v^2/c^2}\]


\[t_\perp=\frac{2L}{c}\cdot\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-v^2/c^2}}\]

title: How This Course Works — and the Ether Problem
text:
Same prefactor, different power
\[t_\parallel=\frac{2L}{c}\cdot\frac{1}{1-v^2/c^2}
\qquad
t_\perp=\frac{2L}{c}\cdot\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-v^2/c^2}}\]
Write \(\beta^2 = v^2/c^2\). Then the bracket is \((1-\beta^2) < 1\), and
\[\frac{t_\parallel}{t_\perp}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-\beta^2}}\;>\;1\]

\[t_\parallel > t_\perp \quad \text{always}\]

The downstream gain never compensates the upstream loss.

title: Events, Frames, and How to Measure Them
text:
Today is unglamorous and load-bearing
No paradoxes. No twins. No \(E = mc^2\).
Instead: what does it actually mean to measure when and where something happened?


Every argument in the next five weeks runs on the machinery built today. The students who find simultaneity confusing in two weeks are almost always the ones who skipped this.

title: Events, Frames, and How to Measure Them
text:
An event

An event is a single happening at a single place at a single moment.



Four numbers: \((t, x, y, z)\)

Two particles collide
A clock reads noon
Light reaches a detector
A firecracker’s first flash













“A firecracker explodes” is not an event — milliseconds, centimetres.



Also not events: “the train” (an object, not a happening) · “3 pm” (a time, no place) · “the collision was elastic” (a description, not a happening).

title: Events, Frames, and How to Measure Them
section: What a reference frame is not
text:
What a reference frame is not

A frame is not a point of view.
A frame is not where somebody is standing.

title: Events, Frames, and How to Measure Them
text:
What a reference frame is
A latticework of rulers and synchronized clocks, filling all of space.

title: Events, Frames, and How to Measure Them
text:
Why this construction matters


Naive picture
One observer, one clock, watching from a distance.
Must correct for light travel time.
Confuses seeing with happening.

Latticework
Clocks everywhere, each recording locally.
No corrections needed.
Data collected afterward at leisure.

title: Events, Frames, and How to Measure Them
text:
Now the hard part
The lattice needs its clocks synchronized.

Two clocks, 300 m apart. How do you set them to the same time?


You cannot carry one to the other — moving a clock changes what it reads, as we will see in L05. You need a signalling method, and every signal takes time.

title: Events, Frames, and How to Measure Them
text:
Einstein synchronization









Flash a light at the midpoint. When it arrives, set both clocks to the same reading.

title: Events, Frames, and How to Measure Them

You synchronize two clocks 300 m apart using a flash at the midpoint. Your friend, moving past at \(0.6c\), watches you do it.
Does your friend agree the clocks are synchronized?
(a) Yes — the procedure is symmetric
(b) No — she says one was set too early
(c) Only if she is also at the midpoint
(d) The question is meaningless

section: How fast is light, and how would you know?
text:
How fast is light, and how would you know?

Galileo tried it. Two lanterns, two hilltops, two assistants, and a shutter.
He concluded only that light is “if not instantaneous, extraordinarily rapid.”


What would you need, to do better?

title: Events, Frames, and How to Measure Them
text:
Rømer, 1676 — the first number


Jupiter’s moon Io eclipses on a strict schedule.
Except it runs late when Earth is far from Jupiter, and early when close.





  Extra distance across Earth's orbit : 2.992e+11 m
  Accumulated delay Rømer measured    : 22 minutes

  → c ≈ 2.267e+08 m/s
    modern value  2.998e+08 m/s   (about 24% low)

  Wrong by a quarter — and it settled the question that mattered:
  light does not arrive instantly.

title: Events, Frames, and How to Measure Them
text:
Bradley, 1728 — aberration
Starlight arrives tilted — Earth moves while the light comes down.


Like running through vertical rain: you tilt the umbrella forward.



  tilt ≈ 20.5 arcsec
  c = v/tan(θ)
    ≈ 2.996e+08 m/s







Bradley’s value was within about 1% — far better than Rømer’s, and from an effect nobody was looking for.

text:
Fizeau and Foucault — bringing it to the lab



Fizeau, 1849 — toothed wheel
8 km to a mirror and back. 313,300 km/s


Foucault, 1850 — rotating mirror
Better precision — then light in water.



Light is slower in water — Newton’s corpuscles required faster.

title: Events, Frames, and How to Measure Them
section: Michelson made it his life’s work
text:
Michelson made it his life’s work


1879 — rotating mirror, improved · 299,910 ± 50 km/s
1926 — Mt. Wilson to Mt. San Antonio, 35 km baseline · 299,796 ± 4 km/s





He was still refining the measurement when he died in 1931. The 1926 value is within 4 km/s of the modern one — a relative error of about \(10^{-5}\).

title: Events, Frames, and How to Measure Them
text:
1983 — the question dissolves

The metre is now defined as the distance light travels in \(1/299{,}792{,}458\) of a second.

So \(c = 299{,}792{,}458\) m/s — exactly, by definition, with no uncertainty.
You can no longer measure the speed of light.
You measure lengths with it.

title: Events, Frames, and How to Measure Them
text:
The catch nobody mentions
Every method on the last five slides measured a round trip.

Rømer — light out to Earth, but timed against a periodic source
Fizeau, Foucault, Michelson — out to a mirror, and back
Modern interferometry — out and back


We have never measured the one-way speed of light.


So why not put a clock at each end and time it one way?

title: Events, Frames, and How to Measure Them
text:
Convention, not ignorance
Einstein’s response: define the one-way speed to be \(c\) in both directions.


That is exactly what the midpoint-flash synchronization does — it assumes the two paths take equal time.




Not a gap in the theory. Every experimental prediction is unchanged whatever convention you adopt. But it is a choice, and knowing it is a choice is part of understanding what the theory claims.

title: Events, Frames, and How to Measure Them
section: Why not just carry a clock over?
text:
Why not just carry a clock over?

The obvious answer to synchronization: set two clocks side by side, then walk one of them 300 m down the track.


This fails — and how it fails is the subject of L05.

Three things a frame is not


Not a person
Nobody has to be watching. The lattice records whether or not anyone reads it.

Not a place
It fills all of space. There is no “where” the frame is.

Not a view
It measures. It does not see.


So — where is the train’s frame?



“The frame of the train” means the lattice that moves with the train — clocks at every point, all along the track and beyond, at rest relative to the train.

title: The Lorentz Transformation
text:
Thursday’s exit ticket


“At \(0.87c\) a spaceship is measured at half its length, so the hull must be squeezed under enormous stress.”


No stress, no strain: every gauge on board reads zero, and the shorter number is still a correct measurement.

The word to watch is “it only looks shorter.” No. It is measured shorter — and today’s algebra says why.

title: The Lorentz Transformation
section: What the transformation has to do
text:
What the transformation has to do
Given an event at \((t, x)\) in my frame, return \((t', x')\) in the ship’s, where the ship moves at \(v\) along \(x\).







it must
because




be linear
uniform motion stays uniform motion in every inertial frame


send \(x = vt \to x' = 0\)
the ship’s origin is at rest on the ship, by definition


send \(x = ct \to x' = ct'\)
postulate 2: light is \(c\) for both of us


reduce to \(x' = x - vt\) when \(v \ll c\)
Newton works, and we must reproduce him

title: The Lorentz Transformation
text:
Two lines of algebra


Linearity plus “the ship’s origin has \(x' = 0\)” forces the form
\[x' = \gamma\,(x - vt)\]
for some \(\gamma\) that may depend on \(v\) but not on \(x\) or \(t\).












By postulate 1, the ship’s view of me is the same law with \(v \to -v\):
\[x = \gamma\,(x' + vt')\]
The same \(\gamma\) — neither of us is the one “really moving”.

title: The Lorentz Transformation
section: Now let light do the work
text:
Now let light do the work









Both of us must measure that pulse at \(c\):   \(x = ct\)   and   \(x' = ct'\). Four steps:

1. Put \(x = ct\) into \(x' = \gamma(x - vt)\):   \(x' = \gamma(ct - vt) = \gamma t\,(c - v)\)


2. Put \(x' = ct'\) into \(x = \gamma(x' + vt')\):   \(x = \gamma(ct' + vt') = \gamma t'(c + v)\)


3. Multiply the two lines together:   \(x\,x' = \gamma^{2} t\,t'(c - v)(c + v) = \gamma^{2} t\,t'(c^{2} - v^{2})\)


4. But \(x\,x' = (ct)(ct') = c^{2}t\,t'\) — the clocks cancel:
\[\gamma^{2}\left(1 - \frac{v^{2}}{c^{2}}\right) = 1
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\boxed{\;\gamma = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1 - v^{2}/c^{2}}}\;}\]

title: The Lorentz Transformation
text:
The transformation, both directions


Ship’s, from mine
\[x' = \gamma\,(x - vt)\] \[t' = \gamma\left(t - \frac{vx}{c^{2}}\right)\]

Mine, from the ship’s
\[x = \gamma\,(x' + vt')\] \[t = \gamma\left(t' + \frac{vx'}{c^{2}}\right)\]











The \(-vx/c^{2}\) in the time equation is the relativity of simultaneity, sitting in the algebra where L04 spent a lecture putting it by hand.

text:
The crank, turned three times
“One clock, two ticks.” “Endpoints marked at once.” “Simultaneous for me.” — what does each say in symbols?









set

length contraction


\(\Delta t = 0\) (simultaneous for me)
\(\Delta t' = -\gamma v\,\Delta x/c^{2}\)
simultaneity offset





Three weeks of argument, three substitutions. The physics did not change, the bookkeeping did.

title: The Lorentz Transformation
section: Row 2, read slowly: measured, not seen
text:
Row 2, read slowly: measured, not seen
To measure a moving ship you mark both ends at once — that is \(\Delta t = 0\), and a length needs it: mark them at different times and the ship has moved.

Feed \(\Delta t = 0\) into the time equation and the ship gets \(\Delta t' = -\gamma v\,\Delta x/c^{2} \neq 0\).
My “at once” is not the ship’s “at once.” The crew say I marked the two ends at different times, and a late mark on a moving ship lands short.











Neither frame is looking at anything: both used a lattice of synchronised clocks, and \(-v\Delta x/c^{2}\) is how much the two synchronisations differ.

title: The Lorentz Transformation
section: Velocity addition, and the wall at \(c\)
text:
Velocity addition, and the wall at \(c\)
An object moves at \(u'\) in the ship’s frame. In mine:
\[u = \frac{u' + v}{1 + u'v/c^{2}}\]


   0.5c + 0.5c  ->  0.800000c
   0.9c + 0.9c  ->  0.994475c
  0.99c + 0.99c  ->  0.999949c
  light + 0.5c  ->  1.000000c



Nothing you can do gets past \(c\), and light plus anything is still exactly \(c\). The wall is not a rule added on top — it falls out of the algebra.

title: The Lorentz Transformation
text:
Fizeau had the evidence in 1851


Light in moving water. Fresnel’s ether: the flow adds only \(v\,(1 - 1/n^{2})\). Fizeau measured it.


Galileo u+v  :   224,906,231.6 m/s
relativistic :   224,906,228.7 m/s
Fresnel 1818 :   224,906,228.7 m/s






The drag coefficient is velocity addition to first order — the evidence, 54 years early, filed under the wrong theory.

title: The Lorentz Transformation
text:
Where Newton went











Set \(c \to \infty\) and the transformation becomes \(x' = x - vt\), \(t' = t\) exactly. Newton is not wrong; he is the \(v/c \to 0\) corner of a larger law.

title: The Lorentz Transformation
section: If you have never multiplied two matrices
text:
If you have never multiplied two matrices


It is one rule, used four times: row across, column down, add the products.
\[\begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{pmatrix}
  \begin{pmatrix} p \\ q \end{pmatrix}
= \begin{pmatrix} ap + bq \\ cp + dq \end{pmatrix}\]
That is the whole rule. In two slides the letters become \(\gamma\) and \(-\gamma\beta\), the column becomes \((ct, x)\), and the answer is an equation you derived this morning.

For matrix times matrix, the answer’s row \(i\), column \(j\) entry is row \(i\) of the first, down column \(j\) of the second. Four entries, four such sums.

title: The Lorentz Transformation
text:
The boost, as a matrix
Use \(ct\) rather than \(t\), so both entries carry units of length:
\[\begin{pmatrix} ct' \\ x' \end{pmatrix}
= \gamma\begin{pmatrix} 1 & -\beta \\ -\beta & 1 \end{pmatrix}
  \begin{pmatrix} ct \\ x \end{pmatrix},
\qquad \beta = \frac{v}{c}\]



Multiply out the top row — across and down, as promised:
\(ct' = \gamma(ct - \beta x) = \gamma(ct - vx/c)\).
Divide by \(c\) — the time equation from twenty minutes ago.

title: The Lorentz Transformation
text:
Set it beside a rotation


Rotation in the \((x, y)\) plane
\[R = \begin{pmatrix} \cos\theta & -\sin\theta \\
                      \sin\theta & \phantom{-}\cos\theta \end{pmatrix}\]
Preserves \(x^{2} + y^{2}\).

Boost in the \((ct, x)\) plane
\[\Lambda = \begin{pmatrix} \cosh\phi & -\sinh\phi \\
                            -\sinh\phi & \phantom{-}\cosh\phi \end{pmatrix}\]
Preserves something we name on Thursday.











\(\gamma = \cosh\phi\) and \(\gamma\beta = \sinh\phi\). Same structure — one sign, flipped.

title: The Lorentz Transformation
text:
Composing boosts is matrix multiplication


boost(0.6) then boost(0.7)  ->  combined beta = 0.915493
velocity-addition formula   ->  0.915493
Galileo would have said     ->  1.300000   (faster than light)




Two boosts multiply to one boost — the velocity-addition formula is matrix multiplication. Poincaré, 1905: they “doivent former un groupe”.

title: The Lorentz Transformation
text:
What the matrix makes obvious







in equations
in matrices




four coupled relations to keep straight
one object, four entries


“combine two boosts” — messy substitution
multiply, then read off


“does it ever exceed \(c\)?” — case analysis
closure: boost × boost = boost


inverse: flip \(v\), re-derive
\(\Lambda(-\beta)\), and \(\Lambda(-\beta)\Lambda(\beta) = I\)





This is what a change of representation buys: no new physics, a different set of facts sitting in plain view. MTH 309 is the course where that becomes a habit; in L14 the same column picks up energy and momentum instead of \(t\) and \(x\), and that object is what a physicist calls a four-vector.

\[\Delta t' = \gamma\Bigl(\Delta t - \tfrac{v\,\Delta x}{c^{2}}\Bigr)
\qquad \Delta x' = \gamma\,(\Delta x - v\,\Delta t)\] \[\Delta t = \gamma\Bigl(\Delta t' + \tfrac{v\,\Delta x'}{c^{2}}\Bigr)
\qquad \Delta x = \gamma\,(\Delta x' + v\,\Delta t')\]

title: The Lorentz Transformation
text:
Two events are simultaneous in my frame, separated by 600 m along the direction of the ship’s motion. The ship flies past at 0.6c.
On the ship, which event happens first, and does the answer depend on the ship’s speed?
(a) The event at larger x comes first, and a faster flyby widens the gap
(b) The event at smaller x comes first, and a faster flyby widens the gap
(c) They are still simultaneous, since zero transforms to zero
(d) The order depends on the speed: below some speed one comes first, above it the other

title: The Lorentz Transformation
text:
The answer, and the number


gamma at 0.6c        = 1.250
dt' = -g*v*dx/c^2    = -1.501 us
so the event at LARGER x is earlier on the ship, by 1.501 us
  at 0.3c: gap = 0.629 us   (grows, never flips)
  at 0.6c: gap = 1.501 us   (grows, never flips)
  at 0.9c: gap = 4.132 us   (grows, never flips)
L04's train, 300 m at 0.6c  ->  0.75 us   -- half the separation, half the offset



The sign is set by the direction of the ship’s motion, not its size. Faster only means further apart, never reversed.

title: The Lorentz Transformation
section: Don’t take my word for it — Amsterdam 1904, Paris 1905
text:
Don’t take my word for it — Amsterdam 1904, Paris 1905


Lorentz, 1904 — Amsterdam Proceedings, p. 812. There they are, with a spare factor \(l\) still attached:



Poincaré, June 1905 — the christening, and our \(\gamma\) as \(k = 1/\sqrt{1-\varepsilon^{2}}\):




One page on, he names \(t'\): “the variable \(t'\) may be called the local time” — bookkeeping, not time.

Set \(c = 1\) and compare his eq. (1) to our matrix — identical, symmetric in \(x \leftrightarrow t\).

title: The Lorentz Transformation
section: Why Poincaré did not write a matrix
text:
Why Poincaré did not write a matrix

The notation was 47 years old when he wrote that page, and he had read it.








1850 · Sylvester
names the matrix — an array whose job is to generate determinants


1858 · Cayley
the array becomes an algebraic object: multiplication is composition


1884 · Poincaré
cites it: “Les remarquables travaux de M. Sylvester sur les matrices…”


1905 · Poincaré
writes the transformation as equations, its structure as a group


1908 · Minkowski
writes it as matrices: \(x = Ax'\), \(f' = A^{-1}fA\)




He was not missing the tool. He reached for a different one — and “doit former un groupe” is the deeper statement.
